questions.title: What is Python? What are its key features?
questions.titleHtml: What is Python? What are its key features?
questions.html:
Python is a high-level, interpreted, general-purpose programming language known for readable syntax.

  • Interpreted — runs line by line via the interpreter, no separate compile step for you
  • Dynamically typed — variable types are decided at runtime
  • Strongly typed — no silent type mixing ("1" + 1 raises TypeError)
  • Multi-paradigm — procedural, object-oriented and functional
  • Automatic memory management — reference counting + garbage collector
  • Huge standard library and ecosystem — "batteries included"
  • Cross-platform and open source

questions.title: Is Python compiled or interpreted?
questions.html:
Both. The source .py is first compiled to bytecode (.pyc), and the bytecode is then executed by the Python Virtual Machine (PVM). The standard implementation is CPython; others are PyPy (JIT), Jython (JVM), IronPython (.NET).

source.py  -->  compiler  -->  bytecode (.pyc)  -->  PVM  -->  output

questions.title: What is the difference between .py and .pyc files?
questions.titleHtml: What is the difference between .py and .pyc files?
questions.html:
• .py — human-readable source code.
  • .pyc — compiled bytecode, created automatically when a module is imported, stored in __pycache__/.

.pyc makes imports faster (skips recompiling); it does not make the program run faster. The script you run directly is not cached.

questions.title: Dynamic typing vs static typing? What are type hints?
questions.titleHtml: Dynamic typing vs static typing? What are type hints?
questions.html:
• Dynamic typing — the type belongs to the object, not the variable; a variable can point to any type at runtime.
  • Static typing (Java, C) — the variable type is fixed at compile time.

Type hints (Python 3.5+) document expected types. They are not enforced at runtime; tools like mypy check them.

x = 10        # int
x = "ten"     # now str - allowed

def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a + b

add("a", "b")   # still runs -> 'ab'; mypy would flag it

questions.title: What is PEP 8?
questions.html:
PEP 8 is Python's official style guide.

  • 4 spaces per indent, no tabs
  • Max line length 79 characters
  • snake_case for functions/variables, PascalCase for classes, UPPER_CASE for constants
  • 2 blank lines around top-level functions/classes, 1 between methods
  • Imports at the top: standard library → third-party → local
  • Spaces around operators: x = a + b

Tools: flake8, pylint (lint), black, ruff (format), usually enforced in CI.

questions.title: What is None ?
questions.html:
None is a special singleton object meaning "no value". Its type is NoneType. A function without return returns None. Always compare with is.

def f(): pass
print(f())          # None
x = None
if x is None:       # correct way
    ...

questions.title: What is the difference between is and == ?
questions.titleHtml: What is the difference between is and ==?
questions.html:
• == compares values (calls __eq__).
  • is compares identity — whether both names point to the same object (same id()).
a = [1, 2]; b = [1, 2]; c = a
a == b    # True  - same values
a is b    # False - different objects
a is c    # True  - same object

Rule: use is only for None, True, False; use == for everything else.

questions.title: Mutable vs immutable types?
questions.html:
Mutable objects can be changed in place; immutable objects cannot — any "change" creates a new object with a new id().

Mutable Immutable
list, dict, set, bytearray, user classes int, float, complex, bool, str, tuple, frozenset, bytes 
nums = [1, 2]; before = id(nums); nums.append(3)
id(nums) == before     # True  -> same object changed

s = "hi"; before = id(s); s += "!"
id(s) == before        # False -> new object created

Only immutable (hashable) objects can be dictionary keys or set elements.

questions.title: How do variables work in Python?
questions.titleHtml: How do variables work in Python?
questions.html:
A variable is a name that refers to an object; it is not a box holding a value. Assignment binds a name to an object.

a = [1, 2]
b = a           # b points to the SAME list
b.append(3)
print(a)        # [1, 2, 3]

x, y = 1, 2     # multiple assignment
x, y = y, x     # swap without temp variable
a = b = c = 0   # chained assignment

questions.html:
• Implicit — Python converts automatically: 3 + 2.5 → 5.5.
  • Explicit (type casting) — you convert with built-ins.

int(3.9)           # 3   -> truncates, does not round
float("3.5")       # 3.5
str(100)           # '100'
list("abc")        # ['a', 'b', 'c']
tuple([1, 2])      # (1, 2)
set([1, 1, 2])     # {1, 2}
dict([("a", 1)])   # {'a': 1}
int("1010", 2)     # 10  -> binary to int
bin(10), hex(255)  # ('0b1010', '0xff')
# int("abc")       # ValueError

questions.title: Why does 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 ?
questions.html:
Floats are stored in binary floating point, which cannot represent 0.1 exactly. Use math.isclose() for comparison or Decimal for money.

0.1 + 0.2                    # 0.30000000000000004
import math
math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3) # True
from decimal import Decimal
Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2")  # Decimal('0.3')

Use math.isclose() for comparison or Decimal for money. 0.1 + 0.2 # 0.30000000000000004 import math math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3) # True from decimal import Decimal Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2") # Decimal('0.3')

questions.title: What is the difference between / , // and % ?
questions.titleHtml: What is the difference between /, // and %?
questions.html:
• / — true division, always returns float.
  • // — floor division, rounds down toward negative infinity.
  • % — remainder (modulo); result takes the sign of the divisor.
7 / 2     # 3.5
7 // 2    # 3
-7 // 2   # -4   -> floors, not truncates
7 % 2     # 1
-7 % 2    # 1
2 ** 3    # 8
divmod(7, 2)  # (3, 1)

result = "PASS" if actual == expected else "FAIL"

questions.title: What are chained comparisons?
questions.html:
Python allows a < b < c, which means a < b and b < c, with b evaluated once.

x = 5
1 < x < 10        # True
1 < x > 3         # True  -> 1<x and x>3

questions.titleHtml: What are strings? Are they mutable?

A string is an immutable sequence of Unicode characters. You cannot change a character in place; every modification creates a new string.

s = "hello"

s = "H" + s[1:]   # 'Hello' - new object

questions.html:

s[4:]      # 'wright'
s[-5:]     # 'right'
s[::2]     # 'Pawih'
s[::-1]    # 'thgirwyalP'  -> reverse
s[:]       # copy

questions.title: Why is "".join() better than + in a loop?
questions.titleHtml: Why is "".join() better than + in a loop?
questions.html:
Strings are immutable, so + in a loop creates a new string every iteration — O(n²). join() builds the result once — O(n).

words = ["a", "b", "c"]
result = ""
for w in words:
    result += w          # slow for large lists

result = "".join(words)  # fast
questions.text: Strings are immutable, so + in a loop creates a new string every iteration — O(n²) . join() builds the result once — O(n) . words = ["a", "b", "c"] result = "" for w in words: result += w # slow for large lists result = "".join(words) # fast

questions.html:

chr(122)            # 'z'
chr(ord("a") + 1)   # 'b'

questions.title: for loop vs while loop?
questions.html:
• for — iterates over a sequence/iterable; use when the number of items is known.
  • while — repeats while a condition is true; use when the end depends on a condition.
for i in range(3):
    print(i)

retries = 0
while retries < 3:
    retries += 1

    if i == 2:
        continue      # skip 2
    if i == 4:
        break         # stop at 4
    print(i)          # 1, 3

def todo():

questions.title: What is the else clause on a loop?
questions.titleHtml: What is the else clause on a loop?
questions.html:
The else block runs only if the loop finishes without hitting break. Useful for search loops.

for n in [3, 5, 7]:
    if n % 2 == 0:
        print("Found even")
        break
else:
    print("No even number")   # runs

questions.title: range() vs xrange() ?
questions.html:
In Python 2, range() built a full list; xrange() was lazy. In Python 3, xrange was removed and range() is lazy and memory-efficient.

r = range(10**9)        # instant, tiny memory
len(r), r[5], 999 in r  # supports len, index, fast membership
list(range(1, 10, 2))   # [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]
list(range(5, 0, -1))   # [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]

In Python 3, xrange was removed and range() is lazy and memory-efficient. r = range(10**9) # instant, tiny memory len(r), r[5], 999 in r # supports len, index, fast membership list(range(1, 10, 2)) # [1, 3, 5, 7, 9] list(range(5, 0, -1)) # [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]

questions.title: What do enumerate() and zip() do?
questions.html:
• enumerate() gives index + value while looping.
  • zip() pairs items from multiple iterables; stops at the shortest.
for i, browser in enumerate(["chrome", "firefox"], start=1):
    print(i, browser)

names, scores = ["a", "b"], [90, 80]
dict(zip(names, scores))          # {'a': 90, 'b': 80}
list(zip(*[(1, "a"), (2, "b")]))  # unzip -> [(1, 2), ('a', 'b')]
questions.text: enumerate() gives index + value while looping. zip() pairs items from multiple iterables; stops at the shortest. for i, browser in enumerate(["chrome", "firefox"], start=1): print(i, browser) names, scores = ["a", "b"], [90, 80] dict(zip(names, scores)) # {'a': 90, 'b': 80} list(zip(*[(1, "a"), (2, "b")])) # unzip -> [(1, 2), ('a', 'b')]

questions.title: sort() vs sorted() ?
questions.html:
• list.sort() — sorts in place, returns None, only for lists.
  • sorted(iterable) — returns a new sorted list, works on any iterable.

Both accept key= and reverse=True. Python uses Timsort, O(n log n), and the sort is stable.

words = ["banana", "Apple", "cherry"]
sorted(words, key=str.lower)      # case-insensitive
sorted(words, key=len)            # by length

questions.titleHtml: Can a tuple be modified if it contains a list?

questions.title: What are set operations?
questions.html:
A set is an unordered collection of unique, hashable items. Great for removing duplicates and fast membership tests.

a ^ b      # {1, 4}        symmetric difference
a.add(5); a.discard(9)     # discard: no error if missing; remove: KeyError
fs = frozenset([1, 2])     # immutable set, can be a dict key

questions.title: Shallow copy vs deep copy?
questions.html:
• Assignment b = a — no copy; same object.
  • Shallow copy (copy.copy(), .copy(), [:]) — new outer object, nested objects are shared.
  • Deep copy (copy.deepcopy()) — recursively copies everything; fully independent.
import copy
orig    = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
shallow = copy.copy(orig)
deep    = copy.deepcopy(orig)
orig[0].append(99)
shallow    # [[1, 2, 99], [3, 4]]  -> affected
deep       # [[1, 2], [3, 4]]      -> independent

questions.title: What is a list comprehension?
questions.html:
A concise, single-line way to build a list from an iterable. Usually faster than a for loop with append.

Syntax: [expression for item in iterable if condition]

q = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
[x * x for x in q]                          # [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]
[x for x in q if x % 2 == 0]                # [2, 4]
[x * 2 if x % 2 == 0 else x * 3 for x in q] # [3, 4, 9, 8, 15]

Rule: a filter if goes after for; an if-else goes before for.

questions.title: List comprehension vs generator expression?
questions.html:
• [...] builds the whole list in memory at once.
  • (...) is a generator expression — produces items lazily, one at a time, tiny memory.
sum([x * x for x in range(10**6)])   # creates a big list first
sum(x * x for x in range(10**6))     # no list, low memory

Use a generator expression when you only iterate once (e.g. sum, any, max).

questions.title: What is the mutable default argument trap?
questions.titleHtml: What is the mutable default argument trap?
questions.html:
Default values are evaluated once, when the function is defined — not on each call. A mutable default (list/dict) is shared between calls.

def add_item(item, bucket=[]):     # BUG
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

add_item(1)   # [1]
add_item(2)   # [1, 2]  <- same list reused!

def add_item(item, bucket=None):   # FIX
    if bucket is None:
        bucket = []
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

questions.title: Is Python pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?
questions.html:
Neither exactly — it is pass-by-object-reference (call by sharing). The function receives a reference to the same object:

  • Mutating a mutable object inside the function is visible outside.
  • Reassigning the parameter only changes the local name.
def modify(lst):
    lst.append(4)     # visible outside
    lst = [0]         # local rebinding, not visible

data = [1, 2, 3]
modify(data)
print(data)           # [1, 2, 3, 4]

questions.title: What is a lambda (anonymous) function?
questions.html:
A lambda is Python's anonymous function: a single-expression function with no name. It cannot contain statements or multiple lines.

square = lambda x: x * x
add = lambda a, b: a + b
users = [("Ravi", 30), ("Anu", 25)]
sorted(users, key=lambda u: u[1])   # sort by age

Use for short throwaway functions passed to sorted, map, filter; use def for anything reusable.

questions.title: What are first-class and higher-order functions?
questions.titleHtml: What are first-class and higher-order functions?
questions.html:
Functions are first-class objects: they can be assigned to variables, passed as arguments, returned from other functions and stored in data structures. A higher-order function takes or returns a function (map, sorted(key=), decorators).

def shout(t): return t.upper()
def whisper(t): return t.lower()

def greet(fn):            # higher-order
    return fn("Hello")

greet(shout)              # 'HELLO'
actions = {"up": shout, "down": whisper}
actions["down"]("Hi")     # 'hi'

questions.title: What is a closure?
questions.html:
A closure is an inner function that remembers variables from its enclosing function, even after the outer function has finished. Closures are the basis of decorators.

def multiplier(n):
    def multiply(x):
        return x * n      # remembers n
    return multiply

double = multiplier(2)
triple = multiplier(3)
double(5), triple(5)      # (10, 15)

questions.titleHtml: What is a namespace and the LEGB rule?
questions.html:
A namespace maps names to objects. Python resolves names in LEGB order:

questions.title: Global vs local variables? What do global and nonlocal do?
questions.titleHtml: Global vs local variables? What do global and nonlocal do?
questions.html:
• Local — created inside a function, exists only during the call.
  • Global — created at module level, readable everywhere.
  • To modify a global inside a function use global; to modify an enclosing function's variable use nonlocal.
count = 0
def increment():
    global count
    count += 1          # without global -> UnboundLocalError

def outer():
    total = 0
    def inner():
        nonlocal total
        total += 1
    inner()
    return total        # 1

questions.title: What is recursion?
questions.html:
A function that calls itself. It needs a base case to stop, otherwise RecursionError (default limit about 1000, sys.getrecursionlimit()).

def factorial(n):
    if n <= 1:                   # base case
        return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1)

def build_list(n):               # build a list recursively
    if n == 0:
        return []
    return build_list(n - 1) + [n]

build_list(5)                    # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

Recursion is elegant for trees and nested data but uses more memory than loops; Python has no tail-call optimisation.

questions.title: What is a decorator?
questions.html:
A decorator is a function that takes another function, adds behaviour before/after it, and returns a new function — without changing the original code. It works because functions are first-class objects and closures remember state. @decorator is shorthand for func = decorator(func).

import time, functools

def timer(func):
    @functools.wraps(func)            # keeps original name/docstring
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        start = time.time()
        result = func(*args, **kwargs)
        print(f"{func.__name__} took {time.time() - start:.2f}s")
        return result
    return wrapper

@timer
def run_test():
    time.sleep(1)

run_test()     # run_test took 1.00s

Real-world examples: @pytest.fixture, @pytest.mark.parametrize, @property, @staticmethod, @functools.lru_cache.

questions.title: How do you write a decorator that takes arguments?
questions.titleHtml: How do you write a decorator that takes arguments?
questions.html:
Add one more outer function that receives the arguments.

def retry(times):
    def decorator(func):
        @functools.wraps(func)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            for attempt in range(1, times + 1):
                try:
                    return func(*args, **kwargs)
                except Exception:
                    if attempt == times:
                        raise
        return wrapper
    return decorator

@retry(3)
def click_button(): ...

questions.titleHtml: Why use functools.wraps? In what order do stacked decorators run?

@retry(3)   # applied first
def test(): ...

questions.title: Iterable vs iterator?
questions.html:
• Iterable — any object you can loop over; has __iter__() (list, str, dict, file).
  • Iterator — object with __iter__() and __next__(); remembers position, returns one item at a time, raises StopIteration at the end. Can be consumed only once.

A for loop calls iter() then next() repeatedly behind the scenes.

nums = [10, 20, 30]      # iterable
it = iter(nums)          # iterator
next(it)   # 10
next(it)   # 20
next(it)   # 30
# next(it) -> StopIteration

questions.title: How do you create a custom iterator?
questions.titleHtml: How do you create a custom iterator?
questions.html:
class CountDown:
    def __init__(self, start):
        self.current = start
    def __iter__(self):
        return self
    def __next__(self):
        if self.current <= 0:
            raise StopIteration
        self.current -= 1
        return self.current + 1

list(CountDown(3))     # [3, 2, 1]

questions.title: What is a generator?
questions.html:
A generator is a function that uses yield instead of return. Each yield produces a value and pauses the function, saving its local state; the next next() resumes from there. It is the simplest way to create an iterator and is lazy (memory efficient).

def read_errors(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        for line in f:
            if "ERROR" in line:
                yield line        # one line at a time

def steps():
    yield "open browser"
    yield "login"
    yield "logout"

g = steps()
next(g)   # 'open browser'
next(g)   # 'login'

questions.html:
It delegates to another iterable or generator, yielding all its values.

def flatten(nested):

        if isinstance(item, list):
            yield from flatten(item)
        else:

questions.title: What is the itertools module used for?
questions.titleHtml: What is the itertools module used for?
questions.html:
Fast, memory-efficient iterator building blocks.

from itertools import chain, islice, count, permutations, combinations, groupby
list(chain([1, 2], [3]))              # [1, 2, 3]
list(islice(count(10), 3))            # [10, 11, 12]
list(permutations("ab"))              # [('a','b'), ('b','a')]
list(combinations([1, 2, 3], 2))      # [(1,2), (1,3), (2,3)]

questions.title: What is functools.lru_cache ?
questions.html:
A decorator that caches results of a function (memoisation), so repeated calls with the same arguments return instantly.

from functools import lru_cache

@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def fib(n):
    return n if n < 2 else fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)

fib(100)      # instant instead of exponential time

questions.title: What is __init__ ? How is it different from __new__ ?
questions.titleHtml: What is __init__? How is it different from __new__?
questions.html:
• __new__ — creates the object (allocates it); called first; returns the instance. Rarely overridden (singletons, immutable subclasses).
  • __init__ — initialises the already-created object; sets attributes; returns None.
class Car:
    def __new__(cls, *args):
        print("1. creating")
        return super().__new__(cls)
    def __init__(self, brand):
        print("2. initialising")
        self.brand = brand

questions.title: What is self ?
questions.html:
self is a reference to the current object. Python passes it automatically as the first argument of instance methods: obj.method() becomes Class.method(obj). self is a convention, not a keyword.

class Counter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.count = 0
    def increment(self):
        self.count += 1

c = Counter(); c.increment()   # same as Counter.increment(c)

questions.html:
• Instance variable — self.x, unique to each object.
  • Class variable — defined in the class body, shared by all objects.
class Test:

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name      # instance variable
        Test.count += 1

a, b = Test("login"), Test("logout")
a.name, b.name, Test.count    # ('login', 'logout', 2)

Trap: a.count = 10 creates a new instance variable on a; Test.count is unchanged.

questions.title: What is @property ?
questions.html:
It lets you access a method like an attribute and add validation through getter/setter/deleter, without changing how callers use it.

class Account:
    def __init__(self, balance):
        self._balance = balance

    @property
    def balance(self):            # getter -> acc.balance
        return self._balance

    @balance.setter
    def balance(self, value):     # setter -> acc.balance = 50
        if value < 0:
            raise ValueError("Balance cannot be negative")
        self._balance = value

acc = Account(100)
acc.balance = 50       # validated

questions.title: What is super() and MRO?
questions.html:
• super() calls the next class in the MRO, usually the parent — used to extend rather than replace parent behaviour.
  • MRO (Method Resolution Order) is the order Python searches classes for a method, computed by the C3 linearisation algorithm. See it with Class.__mro__ or Class.mro().
class A:
    def hi(self): return "A"
class B(A):
    def hi(self): return "B"
class C(A):
    def hi(self): return "C"
class D(B, C):          # diamond problem
    pass

D().hi()     # 'B'
D.__mro__    # (D, B, C, A, object)

questions.titleHtml: What is polymorphism and duck typing?

Polymorphism — the same interface works with different types. Duck typing — Python cares whether an object has the method, not what class it is: "if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it is a duck".

    def launch(self): return "Launching Chrome"
class Firefox:
    def launch(self): return "Launching Firefox"

for browser in (Chrome(), Firefox()):
    print(browser.launch())   # no common parent needed

len("abc"), len([1, 2]), len({"a": 1})   # built-in polymorphism

questions.title: Method overloading vs method overriding?
questions.html:
• Overloading — same name, different parameters, same class. Python does not support it directly; the last definition wins. Achieve it with default args, *args, or functools.singledispatchmethod.
  • Overriding — child class redefines a parent method with the same name. Fully supported.
class Calc:                      # overloading via defaults
    def add(self, a, b=0, c=0):
        return a + b + c
Calc().add(1), Calc().add(1, 2), Calc().add(1, 2, 3)

class Parent:
    def show(self): return "Parent"
class Child(Parent):
    def show(self): return "Child"   # overriding

questions.title: What are dunder (magic) methods? What is operator overloading?
questions.titleHtml: What are dunder (magic) methods? What is operator overloading?
questions.html:
Dunder methods (__init__, __len__, __add__, __eq__, __str__) are special methods Python calls behind the scenes. Operator overloading means implementing those dunders so operators like +, ==, < work with your class.

class Money:
    def __init__(self, amt): self.amt = amt
    def __add__(self, other): return Money(self.amt + other.amt)  # +
    def __eq__(self, other):  return self.amt == other.amt        # ==
    def __lt__(self, other):  return self.amt < other.amt         # <
    def __len__(self):        return len(str(self.amt))           # len()
    def __str__(self):        return f"Rs {self.amt}"

print(Money(100) + Money(50))     # Rs 150

questions.title: __str__ vs __repr__ ?
questions.html:
• __str__ — readable, for end users; used by print() and str().
  • __repr__ — unambiguous, for developers; used in the shell, lists and repr(). Ideally looks like code that recreates the object.

If only __repr__ is defined, print() falls back to it.

class User:
    def __init__(self, name): self.name = name
    def __str__(self):  return f"User {self.name}"
    def __repr__(self): return f"User(name={self.name!r})"

u = User("Ravi")
print(u)       # User Ravi
[u]            # [User(name='Ravi')]

questions.html:
• Inheritance — "is-a" relationship (LoginPage is a BasePage).

questions.title: How are exceptions handled in Python?
questions.titleHtml: How are exceptions handled in Python?
questions.html:
With try / except / else / finally:

  • try — code that may fail
  • except — runs if a matching exception occurs
  • else — runs only if no exception occurred
  • finally — always runs; used for cleanup (close browser, DB connection)
try:
    result = 10 / int("0")
except ZeroDivisionError as e:
    print("Cannot divide by zero:", e)
except (ValueError, TypeError):
    print("Bad input")
else:
    print("Success:", result)
finally:
    print("Cleanup always runs")

Catch specific exceptions first; avoid bare except: because it hides real bugs (and even catches KeyboardInterrupt).

questions.title: What is a context manager?
questions.html:
An object that sets up and tears down a resource automatically using with. It implements __enter__() (setup) and __exit__() (cleanup, runs even on error).

class Timer:
    def __enter__(self):
        import time
        self.start = time.time()
        return self
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb):
        import time
        print(f"Took {time.time() - self.start:.2f}s")
        return False          # don't suppress exceptions

with Timer():
    run_suite()

Simpler version with contextlib:

from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def browser_session():
    driver = start_browser()
    try:
        yield driver          # body of 'with' runs here
    finally:
        driver.quit()         # always cleaned up

with browser_session() as d:
    d.get("https://example.com")

questions.title: What is pickling and unpickling?
questions.html:
• Pickling (serialisation) — Python object → byte stream with pickle.dump() / dumps().
  • Unpickling (deserialisation) — byte stream → Python object with pickle.load() / loads().
import pickle
config = {"env": "qa", "browsers": ["chrome", "firefox"]}
with open("config.pkl", "wb") as f:
    pickle.dump(config, f)
with open("config.pkl", "rb") as f:
    loaded = pickle.load(f)
loaded == config     # True

Never unpickle data from an untrusted source — it can execute arbitrary code.

questions.title: How does Python manage memory?
questions.html:
Python manages memory automatically in a private heap:

  1. The memory manager allocates heap space; small objects (≤ 512 bytes) use the fast pymalloc allocator.
  2. Variables are references — a = 10 creates an int object on the heap; a points to it.
  3. Reference counting — each object tracks how many references point to it; at zero it is freed immediately.
  4. Garbage collector — frees objects stuck in reference cycles.
  5. Caching / interning — small ints (-5 to 256) and some strings are reused.
import sys
a = []
b = a
sys.getrefcount(a)   # 3 -> a, b and the function argument

questions.title: How does garbage collection work? How do you control it?
questions.titleHtml: How does garbage collection work? How do you control it?
questions.html:
• Reference counting (primary) — frees an object as soon as its count reaches 0.
  • Generational cyclic GC (backup) — detects reference cycles such as a.ref = b; b.ref = a. Objects live in 3 generations (0, 1, 2); new objects start in gen 0, survivors move to older generations, which are scanned less often because most objects die young.
import gc
gc.collect()            # force a collection, returns objects freed
gc.disable(); gc.enable()
gc.get_threshold()      # when each generation is collected
gc.get_count()          # current counts per generation
del obj                 # removes a reference, not necessarily the object

a is b               # True  - cached
a = 1000; b = 1000
a == b               # True
a is b               # may be False - don't use 'is' for values

sys.intern("hello")  # force interning

questions.title: What is the GIL (Global Interpreter Lock)?
questions.titleHtml: What is the GIL (Global Interpreter Lock)?
questions.html:
The GIL is a mutex in CPython that allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time, even on multi-core CPUs. It exists because CPython's reference counting is not thread-safe.

  • CPU-bound work gets no speed-up from threads.
  • I/O-bound work does benefit — a thread releases the GIL while waiting on network, disk or browser.
  • Workaround for CPU work: multiprocessing (each process has its own GIL), or C extensions like NumPy.
  • Python 3.13 added an optional, experimental free-threaded build without the GIL; standard CPython still has it.

It exists because CPython's reference counting is not thread-safe. CPU-bound work gets no speed-up from threads. I/O-bound work does benefit — a thread releases the GIL while waiting on network, disk or browser. Workaround for CPU work: multiprocessing (each process has its own GIL), or C extensions like NumPy. Python 3.13 added an optional, experimental free-threaded build without the GIL; standard CPython still has it.

questions.title: What is a race condition? How do you prevent it?
questions.titleHtml: What is a race condition? How do you prevent it?
questions.html:
A race condition happens when threads update shared data at the same time and the result depends on timing. Prevent it with a Lock.

import threading
counter = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def increment():
    global counter
    for _ in range(100_000):
        with lock:              # only one thread at a time
            counter += 1

threads = [threading.Thread(target=increment) for _ in range(4)]
for t in threads: t.start()
for t in threads: t.join()
print(counter)                  # 400000

questions.title: What is asyncio? When should you use it?
questions.titleHtml: What is asyncio? When should you use it?
questions.html:
asyncio gives single-threaded concurrency using an event loop. async def defines a coroutine; await pauses it while waiting for I/O so other coroutines can run. Best for many concurrent I/O tasks (thousands of HTTP calls, websockets). Playwright has a full async API.

import asyncio

async def fetch(i):
    await asyncio.sleep(1)       # non-blocking wait
    return i

async def main():
    results = await asyncio.gather(*(fetch(i) for i in range(5)))
    print(results)               # ~1 second total, not 5

asyncio.run(main())
Model Best for

Threads I/O tasks with blocking libraries
Processes CPU-heavy work

questions.title: What is mocking? How do you mock in Python?
questions.titleHtml: What is mocking? How do you mock in Python?
questions.html:
Mocking replaces a real dependency (API, DB, time) with a fake object so the unit is tested in isolation. Use unittest.mock (or pytest's monkeypatch / pytest-mock).

from unittest.mock import patch, MagicMock

def get_user_name(uid):
    return requests.get(f"/users/{uid}").json()["name"]

@patch("requests.get")
def test_get_user_name(mock_get):
    mock_get.return_value.json.return_value = {"name": "Ravi"}
    assert get_user_name(1) == "Ravi"
    mock_get.assert_called_once_with("/users/1")

Patch the name where it is looked up, not where it is defined.

questions.title: Check balanced parentheses
questions.html:
Use a stack: push openers, pop and match on closers.

def is_balanced(s):
    pairs = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}
    stack = []
    for ch in s:
        if ch in "([{":
            stack.append(ch)
        elif ch in pairs:
            if not stack or stack.pop() != pairs[ch]:
                return False
    return not stack

questions.title: Bubble sort
questions.html:
Repeatedly swap adjacent items that are out of order. O(n²).

def bubble_sort(arr):
    n = len(arr)
    for i in range(n):
        swapped = False
        for j in range(n - i - 1):
            if arr[j] > arr[j + 1]:
                arr[j], arr[j + 1] = arr[j + 1], arr[j]
                swapped = True
        if not swapped:          # already sorted
            break
    return arr

questions.title: Binary search
questions.html:
Works on a sorted list. Halve the search range each step. O(log n).

def binary_search(arr, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(arr) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if arr[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if arr[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    return -1
